conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Dr. Martinez, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician here. I’ll be walking you through a quick check-in called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a 10-question tool that helps us see how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived.

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about safety. There are no right or wrong answers, and many new parents find it a relief to have their feelings heard. We’ll go one question at a time, focusing on the past seven days. Ready to begin?

Thinking about this past week, overall have you been able to enjoy things, or has even the good stuff felt kind of flat?

Honestly, most things feel pretty flat. I still try to do little things—like watching a show I used to love—but even when I laugh, it feels kind of hollow. I’ll be holding the baby and think, “I should be soaking this up,” but it’s like I’m just going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes I’ll catch myself laughing—like when my husband made that silly face changing her diaper—but the laugh fades fast and I’m right back to this heavy feeling. It’s like I have to remind myself, “Oh, this is supposed to be fun,” instead of actually feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little plans—like meeting a friend for coffee or even just taking the baby for a walk—but now it feels like, “What’s the point?” I still do them, but it’s more because I think I should, not because I’m actually looking forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… if she fusses for more than a few minutes I keep thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding her right or I missed some cue. My head knows babies cry, but I still hear this voice saying, “You’re her mom, you should know how to fix it.” It’s exhausting.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be rocking her and suddenly picture her blanket creeping up over her face, or I’ll think I hear her stop breathing on the monitor. I know it’s unlikely, but I still have to check three, four times. The worries just pop in and I can’t shut them off right away.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes—sometimes out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get a full breath, even when nothing’s happening. Last night I was folding her onesies and suddenly pictured her getting hurt years from now, and my chest got tight. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It’s like there’s this constant weight on my chest—laundry, feedings, trying to sleep. I’ll start one chore, remember three others, and just freeze. Sometimes I end up crying in the nursery because everything feels too big and I can’t see it getting easier.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights this week. I’ll finally get her down, crawl into bed myself, and then my mind starts spinning—did I wash the bottles, is she still breathing, am I already failing her? I can lie there for an hour or two before I drift off, and if she wakes up I’m right back to wide-awake worry.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time. I’ll be nursing her and just feel this wave of sadness hit—I love her so much, but I still feel empty. It isn’t tears-all-day bad, yet most moments carry this gray cloud, and I catch myself counting the hours until bedtime so I can breathe.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’d say once, maybe twice this week. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk and just sat on the floor and sobbed. It wasn’t really about the milk—it was like that tiny thing snapped the last bit of strength I had. The tears come fast, then they stop, but it leaves me feeling drained.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It’s… it’s crossed my mind a couple times, just brief flashes—like, “What if I weren’t here?” or imagining driving into the guardrail on the way to her check-up. There’s no plan, I don’t want to leave her, but the pictures pop in and scare me. I try to push them away and focus on her toes or her breathing, anything real.

Hearing how your days have felt since your baby arrived, it's clear you're carrying a heavy emotional load. You described laughing with your husband but the joy slipping away, feeling that most things are pointless, and blaming yourself whenever your daughter fusses. You shared intrusive worries about her safety, sudden panic sensations, and a constant weight on your chest that leaves you frozen and tearful. Sleep is hard to come by because your mind races, and although you love her deeply, a gray cloud of sadness hangs over even sweet moments. Occasional scary "what-if" thoughts about not being here have popped in, and you try hard to push them away by focusing on her tiny toes.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient can occasionally laugh but the enjoyment is fleeting and overshadowed by persistent low mood, matching 'Definitely not so much now'.</sym>, <sym>Her "What's the point?" and doing things only out of obligation map semantically to "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient frequently blames herself for baby's fussing, aligning with "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient experiences intrusive, repetitive worries daily that compel repeated checking, indicating anxiety 'very often'.</sym>, <sym>Response clearly describes sudden panic symptoms with racing heart and breathlessness "sometimes," which aligns with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, task paralysis, and tearful hopelessness, aligning with 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to pervasive worry, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent sadness "a lot of the time" and "most moments carry this gray cloud," aligning with "Yes, quite often."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, intrusive self-harm images that frighten her; frequency is occasional, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 23 (item-10 score 2) places you well above the 14-point cutoff that flags probable major depression. You meet core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most days (<quote>most moments carry this gray cloud</quote>), markedly diminished interest (<quote>what's the point?</quote>), guilt, concentration trouble, sleep loss, and recurrent self-harm ideation without intent. High anxiety items (Q4, Q5) and daily overwhelm support probable comorbid <med>postpartum anxiety</mod>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>OB-GYN</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>psychiatrist</med> to discuss safety and treatment options
2. Ask about starting evidence-based treatment such as <med>CBT</med> or an <med>SSRI compatible with breastfeeding</med>
3. Plan with a trusted adult for additional home help so you can get four-to-five-hour stretches of sleep
4. Call 988 (US) or your local crisis line if self-harm images intensify or you feel you might act on them
5. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress after interventions begin
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based interview

Symptoms endorsed (maternal report in first-person quotes below):

1. Anhedonia: “laugh fades fast… have to remind myself this is supposed to be fun”  
2. Loss of anticipatory enjoyment: “What’s the point?”  
3. Excessive guilt / self-blame: “I must be doing something wrong… you’re her mom, you should know”  
4. Generalized anxiety & intrusive worries: “worries just pop in and I can’t shut them off”  
5. Panic-type episodes: “heart racing… chest got tight… passes after a few minutes”  
6. Feeling overwhelmed: “constant weight on my chest… everything feels too big”  
7. Mood-congruent insomnia: “mind starts spinning… lie there for an hour or two”  
8. Persistent sad / empty mood: “most moments carry this gray cloud”  
9. Crying spells: “once, maybe twice this week… tiny thing snapped the last bit of strength”  
10. Passive self-harm ideation (no plan, no intent): “brief flashes—‘What if I weren’t here?’… pictures pop in and scare me”

Pattern: Symptoms present most days, interfere with functioning, began post-delivery.

Risk flags  
- Recurrent thoughts of self-harm (safety concern)  
- Sleep disruption linked to anxious ruminations  
- Marked guilt, low mood, anhedonia, overwhelm, and panic-type symptoms consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety.

Screening impression  
High likelihood of postpartum major depressive episode with anxious features; immediate safety assessment and follow-up evaluation recommended.
